### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, Walker and co-workers describe the use of supercharged fluorescent proteins, which
have been developed previously to have highly negative surface charge, to bind the luminescent
lanthanides Tb, Tm, and Dy. The authors take advantage of a less frequently used approach of having the
lanthanide emission transfer energy to the fluorescent proteins, altering the emission of the proteins
and resulting in a ratiometric response to the lanthanides. They also carry out experiments with Al and
Fe to assess selectivity. This is an interesting paper overall, exploiting an indeed underutilized format for
lanthanide luminescence. I believe the authors should have tested selectivity and potential for
interferences more stringently. Because the lanthanide binding sites are generic, some conditions (lower
pH, other competing metals) will likely interfere with sensor response, and the authors need to assess
these more completely under conditions more relevant to an actual use case. These suggested
experiments are described in more detail below, particularly in reference to p. 12.
Detailed comments:
Abstract, line 8: I think the authors should be careful about using the word “novel” to describe the
lanthanide-to-chromophore mode of antenna signaling. One example of precedent for a Tb chelate as
donor and GFP as acceptor, which is the same basic principle used here, is ref. 36, Rajapakse et al., PNAS.
2010, 107, 13582. This strategy is indeed “underutilized,” as the authors write in line 265; that is more
correct than “novel.”
Line 29: “the absence of a high-affinity system with appropriate sensitivity for detecting lanthanides both
in vitro and in vivo poses a significant barrier…” I would suggest that this sentence is not correct. The
LanM-based sensors (high affinity) have been shown to work in vivo (the LaMP1 sensor) and in vitro
(TrpLanM, e.g. in acid mine drainage). The authors’ perspective that LanM is too high affinity for certain
applications is valid, but I would argue that the authors have not shown yet that their sensors have
sufficiently high affinity and selectivity to work in relevant conditions. Roughly 100 µM affinity at neutral
pH is likely not going to be sufficient below pH 5 or so, and possibly not selective enough to outcompete
the much higher concentrations of other metals in typical samples. I would also suggest that it is rather
unlikely that a sensor with 100 µM affinity will work in cells because of the presence of stronger ligands
like phosphate, citrate, etc. See below for additional comments related to this point.
Line 57 and Discussion: “[LanM-based sensors’] superlative nature limits its utility as biosensor at greater
than picomolar scales of lanthanide occupancy in more concentrated environmental streams.” An upper
limit of detection will be condition dependent. Under conditions similar to those the authors tested
(roughly 3 µM protein), the TrpLanM sensor’s upper limit of detection would be 6 µM, not 10 nM
(Discussion, top of p. 19).
Line 167: On the point of the CFP series of sensors not performing as well as expected, did the authors
try the other visible-emitting lanthanides, Sm and Eu, which might be compatible with one or more of
the FPs as well? If so, do they interfere with detection? And relatedly, can the authors comment on
whether there might be a way to discriminate between the signals for the various lanthanides that the
sensors respond to?
Figure 3 and 4 legends: the authors need to provide more information (e.g., the experimental conditions)
in these legends. In Figure 4, it is particularly important to provide the protein concentration (0.1
mg/mL? But micromolar would be more useful than mg/mL), buffer, and pH. In my opinion, nanomolar is
a confusing x-axis unit to use for the binding plots as there is micromolar protein and millimolar metal.
p. 12 and following. I am concerned that the authors did not consider a few things when assessing
selectivity. The direct competition experiments never look at an excess of the potential interferent,
which is a much more realistic scenario than what the authors test: 1 mM Tb and only up to 1 mM Al and
Fe. Al3+ is not very soluble at pH 7 and Fe2+ will be readily oxidized to insoluble Fe3+. So it is unclear
how much of these ions are available to compete against the Tb. It is also important to test ions other
than Al3+ and Fe2+. In most sources, there will be far more (10x or greater) other lanthanides like La
and Ce that would likely compete well with the low amounts of Tb, Dy, and Tm. Tb and Tm are two of the
rarest lanthanides. Being heavier lanthanides, Tb, Dy, and Tm likely would have somewhat higher affinity
than the lighter lanthanides, but perhaps not enough to overcome the much higher concentrations. Also,
most sources have high concentrations of other ions that are probably reasonably good competitors for
generic carboxylate sites: Zn, Cu, Ca, Mn, Mg. For example, in ref. 23, there was 20 nM Tb out of the 2
µM total REEs and >10 mM total interferents like Mg, Mn, and Al, and the pH was 3.2. The authors
should test lower pHs than 7 too. I think these experiments are important to demonstrate utility.
I felt the last section, “Higher order structures can also detect lanthanides,” detracted from the overall
presentation as it did not seem to be particularly successful. Perhaps it could go in the SI instead.
Other comments:
Line 46: LanM is not a transporter. I would perhaps call it instead a periplasmic protein with a role in
lanthanide usage
p. 3, ref. 22: I suggest citing the primary research paper in ACS Cent Sci that demonstrates rare earth
separation, rather than the “News and Views”-type article summarizing that work
Figure 2B: Do the authors have evidence that lanthanides bind at the specific positions indicated in the
figure? If not, the authors may want to clarify that their figure is illustrative of possible interactions.
The authors should report the Kds, which seem to be in the 50-500 µM range, in the text.
What was the ionic strength of the buffers for the experiments? It is generally good practice to have at
least I = 0.1 for metal titrations to minimize non-specific binding.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Walker and co-workers describes the use of supercharged fluorescent proteins as
biosensors that detect lanthanide ions (specifically Tb3+, Tm3+ and Dy3+) in the micromolar to
millimolar concentration range. The engineered proteins are suggested as a potential “biomining”
technology for detecting lanthanides in acid mine drainage or other industrial waste streams. A series of
so-called supercharged GFP analogs, with mutations to increase the number of negatively charged
aspartate and glutamate groups on the surface, were in turn mutated into supercharged CFP and YFP
mutants. A fluorescent plate reader was used to measure the relative fluorescence emission of the
protein when excited at different wavelengths in the presence of varied lanthanide ion concentrations.
The results show a statistically significant increase in the “fluorescence excitation ratio” that occurs when
supercharged GFP or YFP (but not CFP) are equilibrated in solution with lanthanide ions.
The excitation ratio is defined as the observed intensity of a fluorescent protein at its emission maximum
(e.g., GFP at 510−520 nm) upon exciting in the UV region (250 – 400 nm) relative to the observed
intensity when excited at the protein’s excitation maximum (e.g., GFP at 465 nm). The presented data
show that the excitation ratio increases with lanthanide concentration (up to 1 mM) for GFP and YFP,
but not CFP. Moreover, the relative increase in excitation ratio is greater for supercharged proteins than for
wild-type analogs, with the greatest effect seen for GFP(-10) and YFP(-31) (negative number suffix refers
to relative surface charge). As a negative control, addition of trivalent Al ions did not significantly alter
the excitation ratios, suggesting the observed effects are due to energy transfer between surface bound
lanthanide ions and the fluorescent protein chromophores. Additional data shows spectral changes
when multimeric FP combinations were equilibrated with lanthanides.
The results appear to show a noteworthy perturbation of supercharged fluorescent proteins’ excitation
spectra that varies with lanthanide ion concentration. However, the data generated by plate reader
measurements does not support any definitive conclusions about the photophysical mechanisms
responsible for the observed spectral changes. Additionally, there are several problems with the way the
data is presented, the rationalization of the study’s significance, and the manner in which the results are
discussed. Considering these limitations, I cannot recommend publication without
significant additional evidence and revised presentation, as detailed below.
Problem with the study’s rationale and justification.
The manuscript posits that there is a significant need for bio-inspired methods for detecting and
concentrating lanthanide metals in industrial waste streams. Certainly, this claim is justifiable, but the
presentation of prior literature on the subject is confusing and contains unsupported or irrelevant
assertions.
p. 2 line 28: “Biomining presents a sustainable, potentially scalable path towards bolstering global
lanthanide reserves via unconventional sources, though the absence of a high-affinity system with
appropriate sensitivity for detecting lanthanides both in vitro and in vivo poses a significant barrier to
practical biosensing and microbial engineering.”
The concept of biomining is introduced in the 2nd paragraph, which continues to describe
lanthanide photochemistry and energy transfer processes utilized in lanthanide sensing. This description might fit
better in the 3rd paragraph that discusses prior literature on bio-based lanthanide sensors.
p.2 line 36-38: “Due to the requirement of synthetic chelators and chemical modulation, these systems
are difficult to utilize in living systems, cheaply or at scale.”
This statement is unsupported and doesn’t really seem relevant to the purpose of the study.
For one thing, the engineered protein biosensors are supposedly intended for use in industrial waste
streams, not living systems. For another, it’s not at all obvious that industrial scale use of engineered
proteins would be cheaper or more scalable than synthetic chelators.
p. 3 line 59: “Considering that acid mine drainage and other waste streams can contain an upwards of
20–100 μM of total REEs, a sensitivity range congruent with such conditions is needed for practical
biosensing applications.”
This statement highlights a need for sensors that detect lanthanides in a concentration range of 10-100
μM. However, it raises an obvious question as to whether supercharged fluorescent proteins with excess
surface asparates and glutamates would remain deprotonated and negatively charged at low pH.
Problems with data presentation and discussion.
The manuscript attempts to show that supercharged fluorescent proteins exhibit altered fluorescence
excitation spectra in response to lanthanide binding and that the fluorescence changes are due to
luminescence resonance energy transfer (LRET) from excited lanthanide ions to protein chromophores.
However, the discussion of LRET is confusing and has errors. Also, the results and discussion are hard to
follow.
- One problem is that the Figure Captions do not adequately describe the data shown in the Figures.
Figure 3, in particular, should describe the data presented in more detail.
- The supplementary data includes 8 figures, but only 2 (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 8) appear to be
referenced in the main text.
- Another problem is that the description of LRET is confusing or wrong in certain cases, e.g.,
p. 3 line 52: “the naturally fluorescent amino acid tryptophan can be harnessed as a molecular antenna
to sensitize the luminescence of trivalent terbium… Notably, this strategy employs a direct LRET, instead
of FRET"
Here, the phenomenon of LRET is confused with chromophore-sensitized, lanthanide luminescence.
LRET refers to energy transfer from an excited lanthanide ion donor transferring energy non-radiatively to a
nearby absorbing species (e.g., organic fluorophore) via a dipole-dipole mechanism. Sensitized
lanthanide luminescence refers to transfer of excitation energy from an aromatic chromophore to a
coordinated lanthanide ion via a Dexter energy transfer mechanism (followed by lanthanide
luminescence).
p. 3 line 90: “Contrary to the established paradigm, in which lanthanides are the acceptors of resonance
energy transfer…”
If this sentence is referring to LRET, it’s incorrect (see above).
Limitations of the data.
The study relies on plate reader measurements to generate single-wavelength fluorescence emission
data at different excitation wavelengths. With this level of analysis, it’s not possible to make any
meaningful conclusions about energy transfer processes that underlie the observed changes in excitation
ratios.
As far as I can tell, the paper hypothesizes that 1) lanthanides coordinate to negatively charged surface
residues on supercharged GFP/YFP; 2) excitation in the near UV (e.g., 340 nm, 360 nm) results in
excitation of the lanthanide ions via an unspecified antenna effect; and 3) energy is transferred via LRET
from the lanthanide to the proteins’ chromophore. The paper suggests that a tryptophan residue could
act as an antenna to populate lanthanides’ excitation levels. This would account for an enhanced
excitation ratio at seen at lower-wavelength, UV excitation (e.g., 280 nm, Figure 3a), but it does not
account for effects seen when exciting in the near-UV (e.g., 340 nm). The paper suggests (Figure S3) that
unspecified aromatic residues could act as sensitizers, but these residues don’t absorb in this wavelength
range.
Higher resolution, scanning fluorescence emission and excitation spectroscopy might reveal features that
shed light on the underlying energy transfer mechanisms. For example, a scanning emission spectrum of
Tb/CFP in the range of 400 to 700 nm might reveal residual Tb emission at wavelengths longer than CFP
fluorescence (e.g., Tb emission line at 620 nm).
More informative would be time-resolved luminescence detection that could reveal a long-lifetime
emission component that would be direct evidence of sensitized lanthanide emission and LRET.
The Cytovita 5 plate reader used in this study should be capable of measuring time resolved luminescence.
